record.paper_title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems
record.context_brief: Sample splitting for observational study protocols
record.original_question: In an observational study protocol that uses sample splitting, where a planning sample is used to choose outcomes or subgroups and a separate analysis sample is used for confirmatory testing, how should investigators choose the planning-sample fraction as a function of the total sample size, decide how many and which candidate outcomes should be carried forward from planning to analysis, and design sequential versions that allow more than one possible planning sample before committing to the final analysis sample?

evidence.quote: In Section 5, we demonstrated that splitting may be a useful approach for selecting outcomes and subgroups in an observational study. Some problems that have not been well explored for the approach include (i) what is a good fraction for the planning sample based on the sample size?; (ii) how should we decide how many and which outcomes should be carried forward from the planning sample to test in the analysis sample?; and (iii) instead of just having one planning sample and one analysis sample, how can we use sequential analysis methods to allow for multiple possible planning samples before deciding on an analysis sample?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an observational study with a total sample of N units (treated and control), in which causal inference is to be performed via a two-stage sample-splitting protocol. The data are partitioned into a planning sample of size n_P and an analysis sample of size n_A = N − n_P. The planning sample is used (without formal inferential guarantees) to select, from a list of K candidate outcome variables (or subgroups), a subset S ⊆ {1,…,K} of outcomes that will be tested in the analysis sample by a pre-specified confirmatory procedure (e.g., a randomization or sensitivity-analysis test, possibly with multiplicity correction over |S|).

Address the following three design problems for such protocols:

(i) Optimal planning fraction. Determine how the planning fraction π = n_P / N should be chosen as a function of N (and of structural parameters such as the number of candidate outcomes K, anticipated effect sizes, variability, and the targeted level Γ of sensitivity to unmeasured confounding) so as to maximize the design sensitivity, expected power, or another principled criterion of the confirmatory test on the analysis sample.

(ii) Outcome-selection rule. Specify a rule, computed from the planning sample, for deciding how many outcomes |S| and which outcomes should be carried forward to the analysis sample, in a way that maximizes the power of the resulting confirmatory analysis (after any required multiplicity adjustment) under plausible models of effects and bias.

(iii) Sequential planning. Extend the above to a sequential protocol that, instead of using a single planning/analysis split, allows the investigator to examine several candidate planning samples (possibly chosen adaptively) before committing to a final analysis sample, while preserving the validity (Type I error and sensitivity guarantees) of the confirmatory test conducted on the eventual analysis sample. Characterize the optimal sequential rule and the corresponding loss (if any) relative to the one-shot split.

Provide answers, or principled methodologies, for (i), (ii), and (iii).
artifact.status_search_result: Recent preprints address parts of these questions: "Planning for Gold" (2024) gives a hypothesis-screening rule for choosing which outcomes to carry forward in matched observational studies, and a 2026 preprint "Optimal Sample Splitting for Observational Studies" proposes an adaptive rule for the planning fraction in low- and high-dimensional outcome settings. The sequential / multi-planning-sample version (iii) does not yet appear to have a published general solution, so the full triple of questions remains only partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Optimal Sample Splitting for Observational Studies
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes a method to determine the optimal sample-splitting fraction that is adaptive to both low- and high-dimensional outcome spaces.
status_evidence.claim: Addresses problem (i) on choosing the planning-sample fraction.

status_evidence.title: Planning for gold: Hypothesis screening with split samples for valid powerful testing in matched observational studies
status_evidence.snippet: Computes sensitivity values per outcome on the planning sample and constructs predictive intervals to choose which outcomes to carry to the analysis sample.
status_evidence.claim: Addresses problem (ii) on which and how many outcomes to carry forward.
